price_note: Lab401 lists it at €49.99 (~US$54 at time of research). D-Logic sells the plain 'USB Stick' variant direct for €39 (~US$42); Lab401's page doesn't show a USD price so the $65 figure from the first pass looks like an over-conversion - treat $54-58 as the more defensible range.

summary: A direct-plug USB dongle built around the NXP PN533 chip, exposing a libnfc-compatible 13.56MHz reader/writer/emulator. It is the RF front end; all the actual attack logic (mfoc/mfcuk dictionary and darkside/nested key recovery) runs on the host PC through standard open-source libnfc tooling, the same tooling that works with any PN532/PN533-class reader.
honest_take: The MIFARE Classic 'cracking' capability people associate with this device is not unique to it - mfoc and mfcuk run against any PN532/PN533 board, including $5-10 generic breakout modules from AliExpress. What D-Logic actually sells for ~$40-55 is a properly engineered, driver-tested, SDK-documented board and support, not exclusive silicon capability. It has zero standalone mode - without a PC running libnfc it is inert, and it does not touch ISO15693 (iCode/library tags) at all because the PN533 silicon doesn't implement that RF interface.
best_for: Linux/libnfc-based NFC development and scripting
MIFARE Classic key recovery via mfoc/mfcuk from a host PC
Learning raw ISO14443A protocol without an all-in-one tool's menu abstraction
not_for: Anything standalone or untethered - always needs a host PC running libnfc

radios.note: 13.56MHz reader/writer/emulator/P2P controller: ISO/IEC14443A (MIFARE), ISO/IEC14443B, FeliCa, ISO18092 P2P. PN533 is the OEM-oriented sibling of the more commonly seen PN532/PN5321A3HN, adding a second UART and higher-current RF driver for reader-module designs like this one; NXP now lists the whole family as 'not recommended for new designs' in favour of the PN7160.

name: GGtag
skill_note: Programmed through a browser-based web-serial badge designer or by playing an audio clip - no toolchain needed for basic use; a Python package (ggtag on PyPI) exists for advanced/scripted use.
build_note: Fully assembled board. Programmed over USB serial, Web Serial in-browser, or acoustically via ggwave (FSK audio) from a phone speaker with no cable at all - a CR2032 cell is required for audio-mode programming.
summary: An RP2040-based e-paper badge (3.52-inch display) that emulates 125kHz LF RFID tags. RFID emulation works by having the RP2040 compile and flash the existing open-source avrfid EM4100-simulator firmware onto an onboard ATtiny85 co-processor at runtime, rather than through any dedicated RFID silicon. It can be programmed over USB serial, a browser's Web Serial API, or acoustically using the ggwave FSK audio protocol. It is a genuinely single-purpose RFID device (LF emulate only) wrapped in a general-purpose e-paper badge platform.
honest_take: It only emulates - GGtag has no reader/scan hardware at all, so it can replay a tag ID you already know, but it cannot capture a badge from someone walking by the way a Proxmark or a covert Wiegand tap can. The '125kHz emulation' isn't a from-scratch implementation either: on each RFID program event the RP2040 compiles and flashes a fresh copy of the existing open-source avrfid project onto the ATtiny85, reusing a technique that predates this product by well over a decade. What's genuinely novel is the e-paper badge form factor and the audio/web-serial programming path, not the RFID capability itself.

Conference-badge-style projects wanting an unusual RFID trick built in

name: ESP-RFID-Tool v2 PRO
firmware_note: A fork of Corey Harding's earlier open-source ESP-RFID-Tool logging project (tracked separately in this database as 'ESP RFID Tool'). Note the original already had an experimental, MOSFET-less 'bonus' TX/replay/fuzzing mode of its own (confirmed directly in that repo's README) - v2 PRO's real differentiator is making TX a fully-supported, MOSFET-driven feature ('clean and reliable transmission' per the vendor) rather than an unofficial experiment, plus wider automatic bit-format decoding (32/34/35/56-bit vs. the original's 26-37bit focus) and being sold pre-assembled.
price_note: €38.00 direct from the vendor (foto-video-it.de) plus shipping from Germany; converted to ~US$41 at research-time rates.
skill_note: Requires physical access to a reader's Data0/Data1/Ground wiring and working knowledge of Wiegand bit-length math to make sense of captures - a red-team physical-access tool, not a point-and-click gadget.
build_note: Ships as a ready PCB with a screw-terminal or pin-header Wiegand connector option. OTA firmware updates over its own Wi-Fi/web UI; firmware is open source on GitHub if you'd rather build your own from the schematic.
summary: An ESP8266 (ESP-12) board that taps a standard 5V Wiegand reader-to-panel wire run, logs the raw bitstream with automatic UID decoding for common HID bit-length formats, and can actively replay or fuzz a captured or synthesised bitstream back onto the line via MOSFET-driven active pull-downs, all through a mobile-friendly web UI. It has no RFID/NFC radio of its own - it works entirely at the wired Wiegand-signal level, downstream of whatever reader already decoded the card.
honest_take: This is a fork of Corey Harding's earlier open-source ESP-RFID-Tool logging project, but the 'v2 PRO adds transmit' framing oversimplifies it - the original already had an experimental TX/replay/fuzzing mode of its own, just explicitly unofficial. What the €38 assembled board actually buys is a properly engineered MOSFET TX path instead of a 'consider it a bonus' hack, wider auto-decoded bit formats, and not having to build it yourself. It only sees what's already in cleartext on the Wiegand wire, which is every legacy HID/Wiegand deployment by design; it does nothing against a modern OSDP or other encrypted reader-to-panel link. The vendor's own 'fuzzing/brute-force' framing and 'qualified professionals only' disclaimer both point at the same thing: this is built for scoped engagements, and casual use on a system you don't own crosses a legal line fast.

Logging and replaying captured badge bitstreams, inline or as a portable unit
Learning Wiegand bit-format math hands-on
not_for: OSDP or other encrypted/modern reader-to-panel links - Wiegand only
Covert long-range capture without physical wire access - this taps the wired reader-to-panel line, it does not read cards over the air itself

summary: VICINO is a bare SPI breakout board built around ST's ST25R3916B multi-protocol 13.56MHz NFC/RFID reader IC, designed by UK studio MCQN Ltd as a mechanically and electrically compatible upgrade path for projects built around cheap MFRC522 (RC522) modules. You still bring your own host MCU, wire SPI yourself, and build firmware against a small (11-star), still-thin-on-docs library fork rather than a mature SDK. At $40 for a chip that street-prices around $8-12 bare from distributors, the premium buys the antenna-tuned PCB, RC522 pin/hole compatibility and OSHW documentation - reasonable if that compatibility saves you a redesign, questionable if you're just comparing raw part cost.

summary: Wiegotcha is a DIY Raspberry Pi 3 rig, descended from Bishop Fox's Tastic RFID Thief, meant to be built into the shell of a real commercial long-range reader (HID Maxiprox 5375, Indala ASR-620, or HID R90) so it can tap the reader's Wiegand output and log captured badge IDs to SD/CSV, viewable over a Wi-Fi access point's web page. It has no RFID radio of its own.
honest_take: There is very little to this beyond a Raspberry Pi, a level shifter, an RTC, and careful GPIO wiring stuffed inside a donor reader shell - the actual engineering is picking a real, working long-range reader to gut and not getting caught planting it, not anything on the Pi side. It does not read RFID itself; it is entirely parasitic on the donor reader's own decode circuitry, so its real capability is whatever that reader already supports. The project is effectively dead: last commit October 2021, the install image lives on an aging Google Drive link, default root/pi passwords are literally 'Wiegotcha', and its own README lists Proxmark3 cloning as an unimplemented 'future plan' - that exact gap is what the separate Gatekeeper fork later added.

But the vendor's own page candidly says the team is 'still testing alternate transmission paths' and has only confirmed basic transmission against one reader model, so treat range/reliability claims cautiously versus the more established standalone MagSpoof devices already in this database.

name: ARD RFID Blocker (Pack of 2) - NFC Jammer
price_note: Lab401's own storefront served EUR pricing during research: EUR19.99 list, EUR16.90 current sale price, for a pack of 2. The $22 USD figure could not be independently confirmed in USD - treat as an estimate pending a US-currency checkout.
skill_note: No setup - slip a card into a wallet/passport alongside the cards to be protected.
build_note: Fully assembled, sealed credit-card-format product; nothing to build.
summary: A credit-card-sized, battery-free card sold in packs of 2 by Lab401 that's placed in a wallet to disrupt 13.56MHz reads of nearby cards (MIFARE Classic/NTAG, generic NFC, EMV payment cards, passports, HID/iCLASS-family, SkiData). Lab401 markets it as 'active defense,' claiming it protects cards placed above or below it - unlike a Faraday sleeve, which must fully enclose each card individually. It does not read, write, or interact with any card's data - it only disrupts nearby reads - so the entire read/write/clone capability list below is 'no'.
honest_take: Lab401's own description - 'no batteries needed, it takes its energy directly from the reader' - is the textbook definition of what the only independent academic study of blocking cards (Alecci et al., RAID 2023) calls a 'reactive' card: a field-powered resonant circuit that only generates noise while a reader is actively energizing it, not a genuinely battery-powered 'active' jammer that transmits continuously. That study found that real-world blocking cards, including some marketed as 'active,' were bypassed in 8 of 11 tested products simply by filtering the card's own (often near-white-noise) signature out of the recorded signal during post-processing - so 'active defense' is best read as a marketing term here, not a technical guarantee. No independent teardown of this specific ARD card was found (only of a different, genuinely battery-powered product, the ArmourCard, which turned out to be a simple coil+microcontroller design), so this classification rests on matching Lab401's own stated mechanism to the published taxonomy, not a physical inspection.

protecting several cards in one wallet without individually sleeving each one
not_for: anyone who needs guaranteed protection against a targeted, technically competent attacker - published research shows blocking-card noise can often be filtered out
true full-enclosure security - a properly-rated Faraday sleeve/wallet remains the more thoroughly validated option
